On Wednesday, April 19, 2017 at 6:12:02 PM UTC+2, Nicholas L. Michaud wrote:

> You're welcome Andrew.  You are correct that the bootstrap filter currently returns the log of the normalized weights.  I can see how having the ESS and/or unnormalized weights would be a nice feature to have though.  I modified the bootstrap filter a little bit so that this information should now be accessible.  The slightly modified bootstrap filter is available here:
>
> https://nature.berkeley.edu/~pdevalpine/nimbleExamples/filtering_bootstrapESS.R
>
> If you source the filtering_bootstrapESS.R file after loading NIMBLE in an R session, the modified algorithm should work by calling buildBootstrapFilterV2(), and will take all the same arguments as the original buildBootstrapFilter() function.  The two differences in buildBootstrapFilterV2() are:
> The mvWSamples model values object that can be accessed after the bootstrap filter has been run now has separate columns for the log normalized weights, labeled "normWts", and the log unnormalized weights, labeled "unnormWts"
> After running the bootstrap filter, you can now call the "returnESS()" method to return the ESS values for each time point.  For example, if you had a compiled bootstrap filtering algorithm named "cMyBootstrapFilter", then:
> > cMyBootstrapFilter$run(10000)
> > cMyBootstrapFilter$returnESS()
> >
> > would return the ESS values from the cMyBootstrapFilter object
> >
> Hopefully this is useful - please let me know if you find any bugs in this modified algorithm or if you have any other ideas for filtering features that aren't currently implemented.  Thanks!
>
> Nick

> On Tue, Apr 18, 2017 at 12:42 AM, Andrew Ellis <a.w....@gmail.com> wrote:

> > thanks for your help. Post-processing the output from the bootstrap filter algorithm in R works well enough.
> >
> > It is possible to have the ESS (effective sample size, for diagnostic purposes) returned as well, or would I have to write a custom filtering algorithm? I had a look at the manual, but haven't figured out how to do that yet.
> >
> > The bootstrap filter returns the normalised weights, is that correct? I would also like to get at the unnormalised weights, in order to get the log-likelihood for each time step (again, for diagnostic purposes).
> >
> > many thanks,
> > Andrew
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, April 11, 2017 at 7:43:38 PM UTC+2, Nicholas L. Michaud wrote:
> > > Ahh that makes sense.  In NIMBLE, elements of a multivariate distribution all have to come from the same vector, so that if you want the position, velocity, and acceleration to be drawn at each time t from a MVN distribution, they will have to be elements of the same vector (i.e. x[1:3, t]).  However, it would be possible to create deterministic nodes that represent position, velocity, and acceleration at time t in BUGS code using:
> > >
> > > x[1:3, t] ~ dmnorm(A %*% x[1:3, t-1] , prec = Λ)
> > > position[t] <- x[1, t]
> > > velocity[t] <- x[2, t]
> > > acceleration[t] <- x[3, t]
> > >
> > > Currently we don't have a system in place to monitor these deterministic nodes in a particle filter (which is what I think you would like), but I think this could be added pretty quickly if it would be useful!
> > >
> > > As a less elegant but quicker solution (and you may already have something like this in place), you could extract samples from the bootstrap filter after it has been run using either
> > >
> > > pfSamples <- as.matrix(cBootstrapFilter$mvWSamples, 'x')       for non-equally weighted samples, or
> > > pfSamples <- as.matrix(cBootstrapFilter$mvEWSamples, 'x')     for equally weighted samples,
> > >
> > > where "cBootstrapFilter" is whatever name you have given the compiled bootstrap filter algorithm that you have built and run.  Then you could use something like
> > >
> > > colnames(pfSamples) <- gsub('x\\[1, ', 'position\\[', colnames(pfSamples))
> > > colnames(pfSamples) <-gsub('x\\[2, ', 'velocity\\[', colnames(pfSamples))
> > > colnames(pfSamples) <-gsub('x\\[3, ', 'acceleration\\[', colnames(pfSamples))
> > >
> > > to replace the column names for easier access.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mon, Apr 10, 2017 at 3:18 PM, Andrew Ellis <a.w....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi Nick,
> > > >
> > > > thanks for your reply. That answers my question, thanks. I was wondering whether state variables could be given names, e.g. position[t] and velocity[t], instead of x[1, t] and x[2, t].
> > > >
> > > > Rbiips, for instance, would allow me to do this. I thought this might make it easier to process the output. Is there an easier way to get at the individual state variables?
> > > >
> > > > Many thanks,
> > > > Andrew
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, April 10, 2017 at 6:26:30 PM UTC+2, Nicholas L. Michaud wrote:
> > > > > Hi Andrew,
> > > > >
> > > > > Particle filters in NIMBLE will always monitor all of the latent states, there is currently no way to specify only a subset of latent states for monitoring (although that's a good idea!)
> > > > >
> > > > > As for using individual nodes for latent state variables, I'm not quite sure if this is what you want, but it could be helpful: for a given time point t, the particle filters in NIMBLE are able to handle state variables that are specified individually in BUGS code.  For example, in a state space model with two latent states at each time, one could specify the two state variables as coming from two different distributions by:
> > > > >
> > > > > x[1, t] ~ dnorm(a * x[1, t-1], sd = 1)
> > > > > x[2, t] ~ dt(b * x[2, t-1], sigma = 5, df  = 1)
> > > > >
> > > > > The only catch is that all of the latent variables at time t, whether specified individually or as coming from a multivariate distribution, have to be elements of the same vector (in this example, x[ , t]).  Also in this example, to build a bootstrap filter, I think you would also have to give the argument:
> > > > >
> > > > > control = list(timeIndex = 2)
> > > > >
> > > > > to the buildBootstrapFilter() function.  This argument lets the filter know that the second dimension of the x[ , ] matrix is the dimension that indexes time.  Please let me know if this wasn't clear, thanks!
> > > > >
> > > > > Nick
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Sun, Apr 9, 2017 at 11:33 PM, Andrew Ellis <a.w....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > is it possible to monitor multiple nodes in a state space model using buildBootstrapFilter()?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > For example, if I'm using a linear transition function in order to model a system's kinematic behaviour (e.g. for tracking an object's position), I can estimate the position, velocity and acceleration in a a 3-d matrix, something similar too:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > x[1:3, t] ~ dmnorm(A %*% x[1:3, t-1] , prec = Λ)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > where A is:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > A <- matrix(c(1, dt, 0.5*dt^2,
> > > > > >               0, 1, dt,
> > > > > >               0, 0, 1),
> > > > > >             nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > and x[1,t] is the position, x[2,t] is the velocity and x[3,t] is the acceleration.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > But is it possible to use individual nodes for the state variables, and to monitor these individually?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > cheers,
> > > > > > Andrew
> > > > > >

messages.subject_clean: Question on data format for Stan in MCMCsuite
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nimblers,

First of all many thanks for a tool like Nimble.

I am using MCMCsuite to compare jags, winbugs, Nimble & Stan on the same model.

I have difficulties with Stan. My main difficulty is with the format of the data and init values that I provide to arguments stan_data and stan_inits respectively.

As an exemple for data I have tried putting in in a list:

ModelData_Stan<- list(Y = tabdivbm3$rssaprotot,x = tabdivbm3$volBMT, Ncases=length(as.factor(tabdivbm3$forest)),xsd = sd(tabdivbm3$volBMT), quantiles_main=quantile(tabdivbm3$volBMT,c(0.05,0.95)),
                    Nforests=nlevels(as.factor(tabdivbm3$forest)),forest=as.integer(as.factor(tabdivbm3$forest)),
                    Nper=tabdivbm3$nb.per.valid,meanlogNper=mean(log(tabdivbm3$nb.per.valid)),varlogNper=var(log(tabdivbm3$nb.per.valid)))

and then written it in a *.R file with the following commands:

format.data <- function (datalist){
    if (!is.list(datalist) || is.data.frame(datalist))
        stop("Argument to format.data must be a list.")
    n <- length(datalist)
    datalist.string <- as.list(rep(NA, n))
    for (i in 1:n) {
        if (length(datalist[[i]]) ==
            1)
            datalist.string[[i]] <- paste(names(datalist)[i],
                "=", as.character(datalist[[i]]), sep = "")
        if (is.vector(datalist[[i]]) & length(datalist[[i]]) >
            1)
            datalist.string[[i]] <- paste(names(datalist)[i],
                "=c(", paste(as.character(datalist[[i]]), collapse = ", "),
                ")", sep = "")
        if (is.array(datalist[[i]]))
            datalist.string[[i]] <- paste(names(datalist)[i],
                "= structure(.Data= c(", paste(as.character(as.vector(aperm(datalist[[i]]))),
                  collapse = ", "), "), .Dim=c(", paste(as.character(dim(datalist[[i]])),
                  collapse = ", "), "))", sep = "")
    }
  datalist.tofile <- paste("list(", paste(unlist(datalist.string),
        collapse = ", "), ")", sep = "")
    return(datalist.tofile)
}

cat(format.data(ModelData_Stan),file="Stan.data.R")

But it does not seem to work since I get the error message:
Error : variable does not exist; processing stage=data initialization; variable name=Nforests; base type=int

The command I use calling MCMCsuite is:

MCMCsuite_RStot.VBM_NBasPG_sigma4p_easa_P_v1_s3 <- MCMCsuite(code = modelCode,  constants = ModelConsts, inits = Inits[[1]], data = ModelData,
                thin = Thin, monitors = params, niter=Niter, burnin=Nburn,
                calculateEfficiency = TRUE, MCMCs = c("stan"),
                stan_model="modelCodeSTAN.stan",stan_inits="Stan.init.R",stan_data="Stan.data.R",makePlot=FALSE,
                debug=FALSE
                )

Any idea on where I went wrong?...

Sincerely,

Frédéric Gosselin

messages.subject: Re: burnin specification with MCMCsuite
messages.body_plain:
Frédéric, I am hopeful that MCMCsuite is doing the right thing. You wouldn't necessarily notice the "burnin phase".  Rather, the initial 1,000 samples are automatically discarded as burnin.

In your example it's slightly more complicated, since the thin interval is set to 10.  So the initial 1,000 samples (out of 50,000 total) are discarded, leaving 49,000 samples.  Then, these are thinned to every 10th sample (the thinning interval), so only 4,900 samples should be returned.  Again, those samples are thinned to every 10th sample, post-burnin.  If MCMCsuite is returning 4,900 samples for each parameter (from each MCMC algorithm), then it's functioning correctly.

If not, then can you please send a fully reproducble example of your code?

Cheers,
Daniel

Hi Frédéric,

First, a couple of general comments: I think it is still the case that to call stan from nimble you will need to install nimble from our web site (see line of code to use at https://r-nimble.org/download).  Also, the feature to call the other packages together has encountered some bugs recently that appear to be due to registration of C functions in R from all the packages together.  Unfortunately we have not tracked that down yet.  If it becomes a problem, you may need to run each one separately rather than in one call to MCMCsuite or compareMCMCs.

Regarding your example: It is hard to diagnose without an example we can fully reproduce.  I will point you to the working MCMC comparisons from the examples page on our web-site.  Here is the first one: https://nature.berkeley.edu/~pdevalpine/MCMC_comparisons/some_BUGS_comparisons/blocker/nimble_blocker_comparisons.html
This is a little different than your case because it goes through compareMCMCs rather than MCMCsuite, but the former calls the latter, with inputs just arranged differently.  The example includes code to download the stan files needed from stan’s github repository and put them on your system.  You can compare to those files to see if you have your files set up and formatted correctly or if there is some other problem.

Perry

Is there a way to reuse a compiled `nimbleFunction` between different R sessions? `compileNimble` generates the code, compiles it, and then loads the compiled objects. Therefore the function would only have to be compiled once, when the user loads the package for the first time. At the moment I compile the function when the package is loaded every time, but this adds a small but annoying extra amount of time for loading the package. I've tried saving the resulting returned object from compileNimble into an .rds file and then loading that, but this doesn't work most of the time, presumably because it seems to be dependent on a symbol in the nimble environment (or something like that)? I'm new to writing R packages, so I haven't got all of this stuff down yet.
I'd appreciate any thoughts on this issue.

Thanks,

Russell

This is something we’ve been wanting to make possible, but it has fallen below other priorities and so remains not done.  Now that you are asking, we can try to kick it up the list.

By the way, you can control where the code and dll are put using the dirName argument to compileNimble.  If you use dirName = ‘.’, they will go in your current working directory.

Is it a nimbleFunction that does not have setup code?  If so, I could set up a quick way for you to do it before we have a more friendly version implemented.  I think all one would need is to use R CMD SHLIB to compile the generated C++ and modify the first argument to .Call in the R function returned by compileNimble to call the loaded dll.

If you eventually want to submit your package to CRAN, we’ll have to work out how to compile with nimble’s headers during CRAN package building.

Perry

Hi Russell,

Thanks for you kind words, as well as patience for follow-up.  I’ve made a wiki page with instructions on how to re-use a compiled nimbleFunction with no setup code. It’s here:

Suggestions welcome.

Perry

> On May 10, 2017, at 4:36 PM, Russell Dinnage <r.di...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi Perry,
>
> Thanks for your prompt reply. As a matter of fact it is a nimbleFunction without setup code. So I would appreciate any sort of hack that would allow me to reuse the compiled code in my package.
> Thanks for the dirName option tip. I had noted that option in the help, but it only mentioned that is where it would put the C++ code, but of course it makes sense that the dll would also go there.
> As far as CRAN goes, that may be a consideration for the future, but at the moment I only intend to distribute the package via github.
>
> And by the way, just wanted to say, nimble is a fantastic package! Thanks for all your and the development team's hard work on it. I've already used it extensively for several projects. So I'm definitely interested in any developments in terms of helping to integrate nimble into other packages, as I have plans for several that would use nimble functionality.
>
> Cheers,
> Russell
>
> On Thursday, 11 May 2017 02:29:41 UTC+10, pdevalpine wrote:
> > Hi Russell,
> >
> > This is something we’ve been wanting to make possible, but it has fallen below other priorities and so remains not done.  Now that you are asking, we can try to kick it up the list.
> >
> > By the way, you can control where the code and dll are put using the dirName argument to compileNimble.  If you use dirName = ‘.’, they will go in your current working directory.
> >
> > Is it a nimbleFunction that does not have setup code?  If so, I could set up a quick way for you to do it before we have a more friendly version implemented.  I think all one would need is to use R CMD SHLIB to compile the generated C++ and modify the first argument to .Call in the R function returned by compileNimble to call the loaded dll.
> >
> > If you eventually want to submit your package to CRAN, we’ll have to work out how to compile with nimble’s headers during CRAN package building.
> >
> > Perry
> >
> > > On May 9, 2017, at 11:20 PM, Russell Dinnage <r.di...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > >
> > > Is there a way to reuse a compiled `nimbleFunction` between different R sessions? `compileNimble` generates the code, compiles it, and then loads the compiled objects. It looks like it creates a file (such as a .dll in windows) in a temporary directory for this. In theory this file could be reused in a new session, such that it would not have to be compiled again if there were no changes to the code. Is this possible? The main purpose I'd like to do this is to use a compiled nimbleFunction in my own custom package. If it was possible to do this I could use the .onLoad function to check if the compiled file exists, then load that, or otherwise compile the nimbleFunction. Therefore the function would only have to be compiled once, when the user loads the package for the first time. At the moment I compile the function when the package is loaded every time, but this adds a small but annoying extra amount of time for loading the package. I've tried saving the resulting returned object from compileNimble into an .rds file and then loading that, but this doesn't work most of the time, presumably because it seems to be dependent on a symbol in the nimble environment (or something like that)? I'm new to writing R packages, so I haven't got all of this stuff down yet.
> > > I'd appreciate any thoughts on this issue.

> > > Thanks,
> > >
